drivingQuestion: If wind-covered blood that stays covered is exempt, why does a baraita obligate covering blood absorbed into the ground?
outcomeNote: The distinction between blood whose mark remains visible and blood fully hidden settles the difficulty.

segments.he: וּמַאי שְׁנָא מֵהָא דְּתַנְיָא: הַשּׁוֹחֵט וְנִבְלַע דָּם בַּקַּרְקַע – חַיָּיב לְכַסּוֹת. הָתָם כְּשֶׁרִשּׁוּמוֹ נִיכָּר.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «But» even if the wind covered the blood and it remained covered, why is one exempt from performing the mitzva of covering the blood? «What is different» about this case «from that which is taught» in a baraita: In a case where «one slaughters» an undomesticated animal or a bird «and» its «blood is absorbed by the ground,» one is «obligated to cover» the blood? The Gemara responds: «There,» the baraita is referring to a case «where the impression» of the blood «is» still «recognizable,» i.e., it was not entirely absorbed in the ground.

moves.summary: The gemara presses Rabbi Yohanan's exemption with a baraita obligating covering blood absorbed into the ground.
moves.about: why blood the wind covered and left covered is exempt, while a baraita obligates covering blood absorbed into the ground

moves.summary: The baraita is confined to a case where the blood's mark is still visible in the ground.
moves.about: answering that the baraita speaks where the impression of the blood is still recognizable in the ground
